title: Block close: a rule of life, rewritten
hookLine: day, week, year, people, world, heart, church
tomorrow: why does the Bible keep counting to forty?

cards: A notes app, a list called my rule, and seventy days of good ideas piled into it: a word on waking, grace at meals, a sabbath, a fast, a letter, a retreat. It scrolls now.

Matthew tells of a man with a list problem of his own. He's a lawyer, an expert in the law of Moses, and he has come to test Jesus in front of everyone. He asks: “Master, which is the great commandment in the law?”
The crowd leans in. One answer, out of all of it.

teach.b: Jesus gives two. “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind.” And a second, which he says is like it: “Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.”
Here's one to tell a friend tonight: neither line was new. The first comes from Deuteronomy, the second from Leviticus, both from the law the lawyer came to ask about. Jesus didn't add a rule.
He picked two and set them side by side.
Then he says: “On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets.” Hang, like coats on two hooks.
Paul says it another way, after a long list of virtues: “And above all these things put on charity, which is the bond of perfectness.”
Charity is the old English word for love, and a bond is what ties a bundle together. So here is the block, rewritten. The day: waking, a word, grace, the examen, sleep.
The week: worship, rest, a fast, a shared table. The year: Advent, Lent, Easter, Pentecost, a retreat. Then people, the world, the heart, the church.
Too long to carry as a checklist. Hang each one on the two hooks and ask: does this help me love God, and the person in front of me? Whatever does, stays.
Whatever doesn't can go. The rule gets shorter, and warmer.

how: Some Christians keep a written rule of life, a simple pattern of prayer, rest, work and service, and review it from time to time, sometimes with a friend or spiritual director.

o: the end of a block, gathered into a short rule
the end of the course, with nothing more to learn
a rule that stops bad habits during your day

p: asks which is the great commandment

s: "love your neighbor as yourself" was a brand-new command when Jesus said it
it comes from Leviticus. Jesus set it beside a line from Deuteronomy.
Colossians calls charity the bond of perfectness
above all these things put on charity, which is the bond of perfectness.
a rule of life, in this block, is a checklist to pass
it's a short pattern to grow along, and each anchor hangs on love.

games.q: your youth group's retreat rules have grown to a long list, and people keep breaking them. the leader asks you to rewrite it. what does Jesus's answer to the lawyer suggest?
o: add a new rule about keeping the other rules.
start with love God and love each other, and keep only what serves those two.
drop every rule, since love doesn't need any structure.
games.why: asked for one great commandment, Jesus gives two and says all the law and the prophets hang on them. the rest stays, hung on love.

practice: Take a scrap of paper and a pen. At the top, write the two hooks: love God, love the person in front of me. Under them, write only the three or four anchors from your long list that hang there, and let the rest go.
If you pray, hold up the short page as it is.

wordCard.voice: Block close. Seventy days of living it, the day, the week, the year, people, world, heart and church, hung on two commandments.

orig.note: the Greek behind 'charity' in Colossians 3:14, the bond of perfectness.

carryVoice: Your line: a rule for love. Two hooks hold everything else. That's the block, closed.
